name: data-mapper
intent: Move all object-to-row translation out of the domain objects and into a dedicated layer of mappers, so domain classes stay persistence-ignorant - no SQL, no table names, no save/load methods - and the object model and the relational schema can each evolve without the other's knowledge.
problem: A behaviour-rich domain model (aggregates, value objects, collections, inheritance hierarchies) structures data as an object graph while a normalised relational schema structures it as tables, rows and foreign keys, so something must translate between the two. If the objects carry that translation themselves - SQL, table names, column mappings, load/save methods - every schema change edits domain classes, the model cannot be tested without a live database, and persistence concerns spread through business logic.
context: Object-oriented applications with a non-trivial domain model that must be persisted to a relational database whose schema does not match the object model - DDD aggregates, value objects, inheritance trees, legacy or normalised schemas - and where the domain must stay testable without a database or reusable across stores (SQL plus document/event storage).
benefits: Persistence ignorance: domain classes contain no SQL, no table or column names and no base class from a persistence framework, so business rules can be unit-tested without a database.
The object model and the relational schema evolve independently - a schema rename, a new column or a switch from one-to-one tables to inheritance mapping is absorbed by the mapper, not by the domain.
Mapping strategies (identity map, unit of work, lazy loading, batch flushing, inheritance mapping) can be layered inside or behind the mapper without touching domain code.
The same domain model can be persisted through several mappers or stores (SQL today, document or event store tomorrow) because the domain has no single persistence dependency.
Schema knowledge is centralised where it can be reviewed and tested once (metadata, generated DDL checks, mapper contract tests) instead of being scattered across business methods.
Loading and conversion rules for value objects, money, enums and dates live in one place (type handlers, mapper conversion functions), which removes the ad-hoc casts at call sites.
tradeoffs: More indirection than Active Record for the same CRUD: every aggregate needs a mapper plus metadata plus wiring, and simple tables pay for machinery they do not need.

Persistence constraints creep back into the domain type: no-arg constructors for materialisation, non-final classes/properties for proxies, setters or friend access for the mapper - the classic failure mode of the pattern.

Mapping errors are often silent and runtime-only (a renamed column yields null, a reordered select list shifts values, missing relationships cause N+1 loads) unless metadata is validated at startup and tested against a real database.

The mapper alone gives no change tracking: to be usable it is normally paired with an Identity Map and a Unit of Work, which adds session lifetime management and its own failure modes (stale sessions, lost updates, lazy loads outside the transaction).
Debugging crosses generated proxies, metadata and session boundaries, so stack traces and identity/lazy semantics are harder to reason about than a record that carries its own SQL.
Load performance is a design decision rather than a default: naive mappers build partial graphs or fire one query per relationship, so fetch plans must be explicit and measured.

participants.responsibility: Holds business state and behaviour; exposes the fields and methods the mapper may use but knows nothing about tables, columns, SQL or the mapper itself.

The pattern's core role, usually one per aggregate or entity: translates between domain objects and rows (find, insert, update, delete), owns column/field correspondence, identity handling and conversions of value objects and collections.

Declares which class maps to which table and which field maps to which column - annotations, an external descriptor (orm.xml, EntitySchema, fluent configuration) or an imperative mapping call - so the mapper can be generic, generated or hand-written without the domain type containing persistence code.
Session-scoped registry of row-key to object ensuring that one row is never represented by two objects in the same unit of work; normally supplied by the session the mapper is used with.
Records new, dirty and removed objects and flushes them through the mappers in one transaction in dependency order; the write-side counterpart that makes a mapper layer usable.
Collection-like interface that application code and domain services use; hides SQL, the mapper and the schema behind domain vocabulary and gives access to the current identity map and transaction.

use_cases: Rich DDD domain models - aggregates with invariants, value objects, inheritance - persisted to a legacy or normalised schema that does not resemble the object model.
Applications that must unit-test domain logic without a database, or that must serve the same model from more than one store (SQL plus document/event storage) behind the same objects.
Teams using a data-mapper ORM (JPA/Hibernate, EF Core, SQLAlchemy, MikroORM, doobie, ROM) to obtain identity map, change tracking and lazy loading while keeping the model free of SQL.
Replacing scattered inline SQL with a mapping layer: schema knowledge moves into mappers so the domain model can be refactored or rewritten independently of the database.
Systems that read and write the same rows through more than one schema version or read/write model, where the translation must be explicit rather than implied by table-shaped classes.
Long-lived products where the mapping metadata is generated or validated (schema inference, DDL comparison, migration tooling) and must be the single place the database is described.
Multi-bounded-context systems where each bounded context owns its own mapper set, and cross-context data flows through explicit translation rather than shared ORM entities.
Event-sourced aggregates where the domain model serialises to a different storage shape (event log, document store) but must hydrate to the same object model.
Legacy schema modernisation: mapping old normalised or denormalised tables to a clean domain model without changing the domain classes.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation requires runtime-decided schema mapping that must be centralised in the mapper rather than embedded in domain types.
CQRS read-model projection targets where the write model uses a different object structure than the read storage, and the mapper must translate between them without coupling.

Microservices with domain events: aggregate state is reconstructed from an event log (event sourcing) but the same aggregate class is also used in services that have a relational store, sharing the same mapper layer.
GraphQL APIs over DDD aggregates where the mapper's projection logic (into DTOs) is the translation boundary between the domain graph and the query schema, avoiding N+1 during query resolution.

Read-heavy reporting where a Data Mapper-backed projection target receives denormalised read-model data that must be stored in normalised transactional tables, requiring explicit bidirectional translation.

Event-driven microservices with event sourcing: aggregate state is reconstructed from an event log but the same aggregate class is also used in services with a relational store, sharing the same mapper layer for bidirectional translation between domain objects and database rows.

CQRS read-model projection targets: the write model uses a different object structure than the read storage, and the Data Mapper translates between them without coupling — projections consume events and materialise through mappers into relational read-model tables.

GraphQL APIs over DDD aggregates: the mapper's projection logic (into DTOs) forms the translation boundary between the domain graph and the query schema, enabling DataLoader-style batching to avoid N+1 during query resolution.

Read-heavy reporting on normalised transactional tables: a Data Mapper-backed projection target receives denormalised read-model data that must be stored in normalised transactional tables, requiring explicit bidirectional translation that is centralised in the mapper.

Schema-per-tenant multi-tenant SaaS: tenant isolation requires runtime-decided schema or connection routing that is centralised in the mapper configuration rather than embedded in domain types, keeping domain classes tenant-agnostic.

Legacy schema modernisation: mapping old normalised or denormalised tables to a clean domain model without changing domain classes, allowing incremental migration where the mapping layer progressively replaces legacy SQL with mapper-managed translations.

Doctrine ORM applications where plain PHP objects stay persistence-ignorant: mapping drivers (attributes, XML or annotations) plus an EntityManager backed by UnitOfWork and an identity map perform the whole Data Mapper stack, which Doctrine documents as its explicit alternative to Active Record.

TypeORM projects in repository (Data Mapper) mode - entities as property-only classes persisted through Repository objects - which the official TypeORM guide recommends over Active Record entities for larger, longer-lived applications.

Java DDD codebases that keep JPA entities in the infrastructure layer and translate them to and from rich domain types with a compile-time generated mapper layer (MapStruct), avoiding the runtime-reflection cost of ModelMapper-style tools.
avoid_when: Simple CRUD where each class maps to exactly one table - Active Record or Row Data Gateway expresses the same thing with far less machinery.
Transaction-script or reporting-style code with little behaviour per class: a Table Data Gateway (or a typed query layer returning DTOs) is simpler and faster to write.
The classes are really data holders without invariants: Data Transfer Object plus a gateway, not a mapper, is the honest description.
You only need to isolate one store's quirks (connection handling, vendor SQL, stored procedures) without a domain model - a Data Access Object or gateway is enough.
A small tool or script with a handful of statements: a hand-written row-to-object function at the call site beats a mapping layer.
Read-heavy analytics where objects are never mutated: project rows into read models with SQL and skip the object layer entirely.
anti_patterns: Anemic mapped classes: mapping to classes that are only public fields and setters makes the layer pure overhead - an Active Record row class would be simpler and just as testable.
Back-door persistence: domain methods that reach for the mapper, keep a session or annotate themselves with SQL 'just for one query', collapsing the pattern into Active Record with extra steps.
Identity-blind mapping: constructing a fresh object per row with no identity map, so two references to the same row are different instances and aggregate invariants break across the graph.

Metadata-driven domain distortion: private constructors, proxies, virtual members or interceptor hooks imposed on the model so that the mapper can work - the domain bends to the mapping instead of the other way round.
God mapper: a single mapper that knows every entity and table, re-centralising all schema knowledge and turning every schema change into an edit of one contested file.
Mapping schema to schema: 'domain' classes that are row-shaped (one class per table, public mutable fields), so the object schema never diverges from the relational one and the layer buys nothing.

N+1 ripple loading: loading a collection then iterating it with a per-item lazy-load trigger fires 1+N SQL queries; Fowler calls this ripple loading - the most common ORM performance killer. Fix with batch or join fetch, not per-item lazy loads.
Proxy identity trap: two lazy proxies for the same row compare as unequal by reference, causing broken equality checks, phantom dirty-tracking and version-check failures without any exception.

Domain model annotation pollution: mixing JPA/Hibernate/EF annotations directly on domain entities contaminates the model with persistence concerns, breaking persistence ignorance and making the domain hard to test or reuse outside the ORM.

Implicit cartesian explosion: loading multiple collections with a single join fetch without split-query configuration produces a cartesian product that silently drops rows or doubles result sets; EF Core's AsSplitQuery and Hibernate's @Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT) are the explicit fixes.

Schema-metadata drift: mapping configuration that silently diverges from the actual database schema (renamed column, altered type, dropped constraint) returns nulls or coerces incorrectly with no exception at runtime; detect with automated schema validation or contract tests against a live database.

Repository-per-table fragmentation: creating one repository per database table rather than per aggregate root breaks the DDD consistency boundary; child entities can be saved independently, bypassing aggregate invariants. The Unit of Work cannot protect invariants if individual child repositories are reachable directly.

Async session per query: creating a new AsyncSession for each ORM query defeats the identity map and causes duplicate in-memory objects for the same database row within a single request; scope session per business transaction.

ModelMapper runtime reflection overhead: using ModelMapper (runtime reflection) for large list mappings (~300x slower than MapStruct) introduces measurable latency in high-throughput API paths; use compile-time MapStruct instead.

N+1 through async-to-sync bridge: awaiting a synchronous ORM operation inside an async function silently bridges to sync execution, blocking the event loop; enable PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 to catch these violations in tests.

AsNoTracking without identity resolution: using AsNoTracking() on queries where the same entity is already in the change tracker returns a second detached copy, breaking equality checks and causing unexpected inserts on SaveChanges(); use AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution().

Global batch_fetch_size over-fetch: setting hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size globally fetches unnecessary rows for small look-up tables; prefer targeted @BatchSize(size=N) annotations per association.

Repository-per-table vs per-aggregate: one repository per database table rather than per aggregate root breaks the DDD consistency boundary; child entities can be saved independently, bypassing aggregate invariants.

Mapping schema to schema: 'domain' classes that are just row wrappers (one class per table, public mutable fields) make the Data Mapper layer pure overhead — an Active Record or Row Data Gateway would be simpler and equally testable.
design_principles: Separation of concerns / single responsibility: domain objects own behaviour, mappers own translation and persistence.
Dependency inversion: the mapper (infrastructure) depends on the domain, never the other way round - the model sits at the centre of a ports-and-adapters arrangement.
Information hiding: SQL, table and column names stay behind the mapper's interface, so the domain's public API is the model's vocabulary.
Open/closed: schema evolution is absorbed by changing or adding mappers and metadata, not by editing domain classes.
Persistence ignorance as a testability seam: because the model has no database dependency, its rules can be tested with plain objects, and the mapping is verified separately against a real store.
Aggregate root discipline: only aggregate roots should have repositories; child entities are loaded and saved only through their parent aggregate to maintain transactional consistency (Evans, DDD).

Interface segregation for mappers: define a mapper interface (e.g., ICustomerMapper) per aggregate in the domain layer, with the concrete implementation in infrastructure; domain code depends only on the interface, enabling test doubles and store swapping.

Mapping as an infrastructure boundary: the mapper belongs in the infrastructure or persistence layer, not alongside domain entities; a build-time or import-time dependency check should enforce that the domain layer does not reference the mapper module.

Read and write separation (CQRS): keep the mapper's read path (domain ← row) and write path (domain → row) logically separate; read paths should use projections and AsNoTracking to avoid unnecessary change tracker overhead, especially in read-heavy services.

Mapper contract testing: test each mapper against the real database engine (not an in-memory substitute) to catch FK constraints, type coercion, nullability and Unicode edge cases that in-memory databases silently ignore.

Idempotent projections: in CQRS/event-sourced read models, each projection handler must be idempotent — applying the same event multiple times must produce the same result. Use checkpoint-based (position) comparison rather than event-id deduplication to avoid storage bloat in high-throughput systems.

Async safety: in async stacks, the Data Mapper must never perform synchronous database I/O inside an async function (no implicit lazy loads, no sync session access), as this blocks the event loop. Enforce lazy='raise' or lazy='selectin' for all relationships in async sessions.

CQRS separation at the mapper boundary: keep the read path (rows → DTOs/projections) free of the change tracker and identity map overhead; use AsNoTracking in EF Core, session.no_autoflush in SQLAlchemy, or dedicated read-only repositories for the query side.

Batch mutation awareness: bulk writes (ExecuteUpdateAsync, ExecuteDeleteAsync in EF Core; direct JDBC batching in Hibernate) bypass the change tracker and the identity map, so they must not be mixed with tracked entity mutations in the same transaction without explicit re-synchronisation.

Mapper interface segregation: define one mapper interface per aggregate root in the domain layer; the concrete mapper implementation lives in infrastructure and is injected. This enables lazy-loading-free unit tests (mock mappers) and store substitution without touching domain code.
best_practices: For async stacks (FastAPI + SQLAlchemy 2.0 + asyncpg/aiomysql/aiosqlite): use create_async_engine + async_sessionmaker, always use expire_on_commit=False, replace all lazy='select' with lazy='raise' or lazy='selectin', and never access relationship attributes outside an async session context.

Choose MapStruct over ModelMapper or Orika for JPA/domain entity translation: MapStruct generates compile-time mapping code and is 10x–20x faster than runtime-reflection ModelMapper, which matters when mapping large lists or nested object graphs.

In EF Core 8/9, use ExecuteUpdateAsync and ExecuteDeleteAsync for bulk mutations (archive/soft-delete batches) that bypass the change tracker; for high-throughput read paths always use AsNoTracking or AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution.

Route all domain-to-DTO conversions through a dedicated mapper (MapStruct, a hand-written mapper or Assembler) in the application/infrastructure layer; the domain layer must never produce its own DTOs or know about API shapes.

In CQRS/event-sourced systems, treat each read-model projection as a separate write-side consumer; keep projections idempotent by using last-handled position (checkpoint) comparison rather than event-id deduplication to avoid storage bloat.

For Hibernate: use @BatchSize(size=N) on collections and entities to collapse N+1 lazy loads into floor(N/batch_size) queries; enable bytecode enhancement (enableDirtyTracking) to shift session diff-walking cost to the entity; prefer Set over List for @OneToMany to avoid MultipleBagFetchException.

Implement mapper contract tests (test each mapper against the real database engine) to catch FK constraint violations, type coercion errors and Unicode edge cases that in-memory databases (H2, SQLite) silently ignore in test environments.

In multi-tenant applications, implement tenant isolation at the mapper/query filter level (EF Core query filters, Hibernate @Where clause) rather than embedding tenant_id in entity types, so domain entities remain tenant-agnostic.

Expose mapper interfaces from the domain layer (ICustomerMapper) with the concrete implementation in infrastructure; domain code depends only on the interface, enabling unit testing with mock mappers and store swapping without domain changes.

For SQLAlchemy 2.0: prefer selectinload() for one-to-many collections (linear query count, no cartesian risk), joinedload() only for many-to-one references (single parent per child); use raiseload() on relationship() to catch accidental lazy loads at runtime in critical paths.

In event-sourced systems, the Data Mapper is a projection target from the event log, not the authoritative state store: the same mapper interface can hydrate domain objects from relational rows for legacy reads and from reconstructed event state for new writes, keeping the domain model identical.

Apply aggregate root discipline rigorously: only aggregate roots have repositories; child entities are persisted only through their parent aggregate's mapper to maintain transactional consistency and prevent invariant violations from direct child saves.

Configure second-level caching at the aggregate-root level only for data that is rarely invalidated and frequently read; avoid caching aggregates with real-time invariants, and always invalidate on state changes to prevent stale reads.

Use private fields with field-based mapping (PropertyAccessMode.Field in EF Core, MappedColumn in SQLAlchemy, @Access(AccessType.FIELD) in Hibernate) to expose behaviour-only public interfaces while ORMs map to encapsulated state, achieving true persistence ignorance.
One mapper per aggregate root (or per entity), owning find, insert, update and delete plus the row-to-object translation for that aggregate only.
Pair the mapper with an Identity Map and a Unit of Work so a row is one object per session and all writes flush in a single transaction in dependency order.

Keep the mapping declaration outside the domain type where the stack allows it (external descriptor, EntitySchema, imperative mapping call, fluent configuration); if annotations are unavoidable, keep them metadata and verify they do not change domain semantics.

Validate the mapping instead of hoping: schema checks or generated DDL comparison at startup, plus contract tests that run the mappers against the real database engine (not only an in-memory stand-in).
Make load strategy explicit - batch/select-in, join fetch or lazy - and forbid implicit per-object loads inside loops; keep a query counter in tests to catch N+1 regressions.
Route every conversion (value objects, money, enums, dates, nullability) through mapper-level type handlers, never ad-hoc casts at call sites.
Keep the mapper in the infrastructure/application layer: the domain module must not import it, and a dependency test should fail the build if it does.
Define transactions at the session/unit-of-work boundary, not inside domain methods, so a domain operation cannot half-commit across several mappers.

Handle cyclic references by registering an empty ghost object in the identity map before recursive load begins (Fowler, PEAA p.169-170); this breaks the infinite-load loop and preserves identity for circular relationships.
Override equals() and hashCode() on entity types by primary key, not by reference, to guard against the proxy identity trap where two proxies for the same row compare unequal.

Use private fields with PropertyAccessMode.Field (EF Core), MappedColumn annotations (SQLAlchemy) or field-access Kotlin entities to expose behaviour-only public interfaces while the ORM maps to private state - this is the modern approach to truly persistence-ignorant DDD entities.
Enforce aggregate root boundaries: repositories exist only for aggregate roots; child entities are never persisted directly but only as part of their parent aggregate's hydration/snapshot.

Test the mapping layer independently with mapper contract tests - load and save each aggregate against the real database engine, verifying that bidirectional relationships, value objects and identity are preserved round-trip.

For DDD stacks with separate persistence and domain models (JPA entities vs domain entities), use a dedicated mapping library (MapStruct, ModelMapper) to translate between them; keep the mapping logic in the infrastructure layer, not the domain.

Choose batch-loading strategy by access pattern: selectin (one extra IN query, safe for collections) vs joined (single query with LEFT JOIN, risk of cartesian product on multi-valued relations) vs subquery (extra correlated subquery, good for @OneToOne). Measure with pg_stat_statements calls count, not individual query plans.

Expose mapper interfaces from the domain layer (e.g., ICustomerMapper) so that the infrastructure implementation is injected; this enables unit testing of domain code with a mock mapper that never touches a database.

Avoid returning managed ORM entities from service/handler layers to external callers (API, message handlers): use a projection or DTO so that lazy loading and session management are contained within the mapper boundary, not leaked across the wire.

Configure second-level caching at the query or aggregate-root level only for data that is rarely invalidated and frequently read; avoid caching aggregates with invariants that depend on real-time reads.

In event-sourced systems, treat the Data Mapper as a projection target from the event log, not the authoritative state store; the same mapper interface can hydrate from relational rows for legacy reads and from events for new writes.

SQLAlchemy 2.0: prefer selectinload() for one-to-many collections (linear query count), joinedload() only for many-to-one references (single parent per child, no multiplication); use raiseload() on relationship() to catch accidental lazy loads in performance-critical code paths; prefer AsyncSession for async handlers and use session.execute() with select() rather than the legacy query API.

EF Core: use AsNoTracking() or AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution() for all read-only queries; rely on the change tracker only within a unit of work that will call SaveChanges(); configure shadow properties (audit fields, soft-delete flags) in OnModelCreating rather than polluting entities; use ExecuteUpdateAsync/ExecuteDeleteAsync for bulk writes that bypass the change tracker.

Hibernate: prefer Set over List for @OneToMany/@ManyToMany to avoid MultipleBagFetchException; use @EntityGraph or @QueryHints for declarative fetch graphs; enable bytecode enhancement (enableDirtyTracking) to shift dirty-check cost from Session diff-walking to the entity itself; configure @BatchSize(size=N) on collections to batch N+1 lazy loads into floor(N/collection_size) queries.
sources: TypeORM - Active Record vs Data Mapper (https://typeorm.io/active-record-data-mapper) — Official TypeORM documentation comparing Active Record and Data Mapper patterns with practical examples; emphasises that Data Mapper approach scales better in larger applications while Active Record suits smaller apps.

Miguel Grinberg - SQLAlchemy 2 In Practice, Chapter 7: Asynchronous SQLAlchemy (https://blog.miguelgrinberg.com/post/sqlalchemy-2-in-practice---chapter-7-asynchronous-sqlalchemy) — Practical guide to SQLAlchemy 2.0 async support covering AsyncEngine, AsyncSession, aiosqlite/aiomysql/asyncpg drivers, lazy='raise' for relationships in async code, expire_on_commit=False, and selectinload vs joinedload in async contexts.

Oskar Dudycz - Guide to Projections and Read Models in Event-Driven Architecture (https://event-driven.io/en/projections_and_read_models_in_event_driven_architecture) — Definitive practitioner guide to CQRS projections; explains left-fold vs batch processing, idempotency strategies (event-carried state transfer, checkpoint-based, inbox deduplication), blue-green rebuild, eventual consistency handling, and scaling via data partitioning per projection.

Vlad Mihalcea - High-Performance Java Persistence, Chapter 14: Batching (https://vladmihalcea.com/high-performance-java-persistence/) — Authoritative Hibernate performance reference covering JDBC batch size configuration (hibernate.jdbc.batch_size), order inserts/updates, batching limitations with identity columns, and batch fetch strategies for collections.

Thorben Janssen - Hibernate Best Practices (https://thorben-janssen.com) — Practical Hibernate/JPA best practices covering projection-based queries, named parameter binding, static strings for named queries, AttributeConverter for custom types, and batch fetching configuration.

Milan Jovanović - EF Core Performance Guide (https://milanjovanovic.tech/blog/ef-core-performance) — Comprehensive EF Core performance optimisation covering query optimisation, AsNoTracking for read-only paths, batch operations (ExecuteUpdateAsync/ExecuteDeleteAsync), DbContext pooling, and N+1 prevention strategies.

Matthias Noback - Simple Solutions 1: Active Record versus Data Mapper (https://matthiasnoback.nl/2022/08/10/simple-solutions-1-active-record-versus-data-mapper/) — Analytical comparison of Active Record and Data Mapper focusing on the simplicity/complexity trade-off; argues the choice depends on team size, model complexity and how long the application is expected to live.

Dev.to - .NET ORM Options & Best Practices for 2026 (https://dev.to/dotnet-orm-options-and-best-practices-for-2026-4a7j) — Current .NET ORM landscape analysis covering EF Core 8/9, Dapper, NHibernate; recommends AsNoTracking for read-only ops, bulk operations in EF Core 7+, and DbContext pooling for high-throughput services.

Chris Woody Woodruff - The N+1 Query Problem in EF Core: Detection, Diagnosis, and Permanent Fixes (https://www.woodruff.dev/the-n1-query-problem-in-ef-core/) — Practical EF Core N+1 guide covering Include, ThenInclude, AsSplitQuery, projection-based fixes (Select + anonymous types), and query monitoring with logging interceptors.

Eugene Kovko - N+1 Problem in Hibernate and Spring Data JPA (https://www.baeldung.com/spring-hibernate-n1-problem) — Hibernate N+1 mechanics covering lazy vs eager FetchType, @Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT), JOIN FETCH pitfalls, batch_size configuration, and DTO projection as a definitive fix.

Chan Le - Data Source Patterns: Active Record, Data Mapper, Table Data Gateway & Row Data Gateway (https://www.chanhle.dev/en/blog/enterprise-data-source-patterns) — Comprehensive pattern comparison with TypeORM examples; discusses N+1 variants (select N+1, join N+1), migration strategies between patterns, and selection criteria for each pattern based on model complexity.

Khalil Stemmler - Implementing DTOs, Mappers & the Repository Pattern using Sequelize ORM (https://khalilstemmler.com/articles/typescript-domain-driven-design/repository-dto-mapper/) — DDD-aligned TypeScript/Node implementation of toDomain/toPersistence/toDTO mappers; demonstrates mapper separation in a hexagonal architecture, with dedicated domain entity types distinct from persistence models.

Stack Overflow - What exactly is the difference between a data mapper and a repository? (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27996119/what-exactly-is-the-difference-between-a-data-mapper-and-a-repository) — Accepted answer clarifies that Data Mapper handles single-object translation while Repository handles collection-level querying and delegates per-object work to the mapper; also clarifies Evans DDD aggregate root rule.

Fabio Fumarola (ed.) - Evans DDD Final Manuscript PDF (https://fabiofumarola.github.io/nosql/readingMaterial/Evans03.pdf) — Digitised Evans DDD chapters on Repositories, Aggregates, Factories and Designing Objects for Relational Databases; foundational reference for aggregate root discipline and repository contracts.

Arxiv - A Systematic Mapping Study on Architectural Approaches for Performance Analysis (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15234) — 2024 systematic mapping study of 109 papers on software architecture and performance; relevant to Data Mapper quality-attribute trade-offs (testability vs performance) and architectural decision-making.

Herberto Graça - PEAA.3 Mapping to Relational DBs (https://herbertograca.com/2016/07/11/peaa-3-mapping-to-relational-dbs/) — Practical EAA pattern context guide covering Data Mapper in the full patterns landscape; maps structural, relational and performance patterns with their interactions and dependencies.

Ivan Málaga - Scaling Business Logic: Enterprise Design Patterns and the Data Mapper (https://medium.com/@im2021071086/scaling-business-logic-enterprise-design-patterns-and-the-data-mapper-c413ff7d7a76) — Python implementation case study of Data Mapper in a security platform; demonstrates mapper layer benefits for multi-store persistence (SQL + document store) and schema evolution over time.

Jigar Patel - Mastering Data Source Patterns: A Developer's Guide to Choosing the Right Data Access Strategy (https://medium.com/codetodeploy/mastering-data-source-patterns-a-developers-guide-to-choosing-the-right-data-access-strategy-ded5e444c758) — Developer-facing pattern selection guide covering when to prefer Data Mapper over Active Record, Row Data Gateway and Table Data Gateway; includes decision tree based on model complexity and team size.

Milan Jovanović - Shadow Properties in EF Core Explained (https://milanjovanovic.tech/blog/shadow-properties-ef-core) — Detailed EF Core shadow property mechanics; covers FK shadow properties, audit fields (CreatedAt, UpdatedAt), soft-delete query filters, and the detached entity limitation where shadow values are lost on re-attachment.

Code Major - The Hibernate MultipleBagFetchException (https://codemajor.de/2025/03/18/the-hibernate-multiplebagfetchexception/) — Root-cause analysis of Hibernate MultipleBagFetchException: bag semantics with unordered Lists, cartesian product risk, and definitive fix via @OrderColumn or Set vs List choice; includes two-query merge pattern.

BookForge - Data Source Pattern Selector skill (https://github.com/bookforge-ai/bookforge-skills/blob/main/books/patterns-of-enterprise-application-architecture/skills/data-source-pattern-selector/SKILL.md) — Pattern selection decision framework; provides selection criteria for AR vs DM vs RTW patterns based on DDD alignment, ORM applicability, testability and operational complexity.

BookForge - Data Access Anti-Pattern Auditor skill (https://github.com/bookforge-ai/bookforge-skills/blob/main/books/patterns-of-enterprise-application-architecture/skills/data-access-anti-pattern-auditor/SKILL.md) — Anti-pattern detection framework for data access layers; covers N+1/ripple loading detection, ghost/proxy identity trap, AR/DM mismatch severity ranking, and remediation priority scoring.

related_patterns_notes.active-record: Alternative: Active Record couples domain objects to their own persistence (the object holds find/insert/update/delete). Data Mapper decouples this by moving all translation to a separate layer. Use Data Mapper when the domain is rich and the schema diverges from the object model; use Active Record when each class is essentially a row wrapper with minimal behaviour.
related_patterns_notes.repository: Sits above Data Mapper in the interface layer: Repository provides a collection-like, domain-facing API (GetById, FindActive, Add, Remove) and delegates the actual object-to-row translation to one or more mappers. Repository also manages query specification (criteria objects, Specification pattern) independently of the mapper's internal query-building. Fowler describes Repository as 'a set of domain objects in memory with a way to find them' that mediates the domain and the data mapping layer. Key insight: Data Mapper handles single-object translation; Repository handles collection-level querying and delegates per-object work to the mapper. The Repository pattern is redundant on top of an ORM that already implements it (EF Core DbContext IS a Unit of Work + Repository); add it only when the domain needs a domain-vocabulary query interface or multiple backend support.
related_patterns_notes.unit-of-work: Companion write-side pattern: Unit of Work tracks which domain objects have been created, mutated or deleted within a session and flushes them through the appropriate mappers in a single atomic transaction, handling cascading and dependency ordering. Without a Unit of Work, a mapper can only persist one object at a time, making atomic multi-aggregate transactions impossible.
related_patterns_notes.identity-map: Companion read-side pattern: Identity Map ensures that within a session, each database row maps to exactly one in-memory object instance. This prevents two queries for the same row from producing two distinct object instances, which would break aggregate invariants and cause inconsistent state. The mapper populates and consults the identity map on every load operation.
related_patterns_notes.row-data-gateway: Simpler sibling: Row Data Gateway gives each domain object its own gateway object that handles all database access for that row, but the gateway returns and receives raw data structures rather than performing rich object-to-row translation. Data Mapper is more powerful and more ceremony; Row Data Gateway is appropriate when the object model is flat and mirrors the table schema.
related_patterns_notes.table-data-gateway: Simpler sibling: Table Data Gateway is a single instance that handles all CRUD for an entire table, returning rows as resultsets or simple data holders. Unlike Data Mapper, it has no concept of domain-object translation, identity or aggregate structure. Table Data Gateway works well as the persistence primitive behind a Repository or as a building block for simpler applications that do not need a rich object model.
related_patterns_notes.foreign-key-mapping: A structural mapping sub-pattern: Foreign Key Mapping represents database foreign-key relationships (one-to-many, many-to-one) as object references or collections within the domain object. The Data Mapper handles the translation of the FK column value to and from the referenced object's identity, consulting the identity map to resolve or register the linked object.
related_patterns_notes.dependent-mapping: A structural mapping sub-pattern: Dependent Mapping places the mapping logic for a child entity inside its parent's mapper rather than in a separate mapper class. Used for value objects and entities that only make sense in the context of their parent aggregate; avoids a separate mapper and query for every child that has no independent identity outside the aggregate.
related_patterns_notes.metadata-mapping: A structural mapping sub-pattern: Metadata Mapping externalises the column-to-field correspondence into a declarative descriptor (XML, JSON, fluent API, annotations) so the mapper can be generic. Data Mapper uses Metadata Mapping to drive its translation without embedding table names or column lists in domain classes. Fowler defines it as 'a structure that holds the metadata for mapping between fields in a database row and fields in an in-memory object'.
related_patterns_notes.lazy-load: A performance and interaction pattern: Lazy Load defers the loading of associated data (collections, references) until the property is first accessed. Data Mapper implementations typically use lazy-load proxies or value holders. The proxy identity trap and ripple loading are failure modes introduced by the interaction of Lazy Load with Identity Map - the mapper must register a proxy in the identity map before the lazy load fires to avoid duplicate objects.
related_patterns_notes.query-object: Companion query pattern: Query Object encapsulates a database query as an object structure that the mapper can interpret into SQL. This separates query construction from the mapper itself, allowing the same query logic to be composed, tested and reused across different mapper implementations. Data Mapper + Query Object enables a fully object-oriented query layer that never embeds SQL strings in domain code.
related_patterns_notes.specification: Companion query composition pattern: Specification encapsulates a business rule or query criteria as a composable object that the Repository or Query Object can evaluate. This keeps filter logic declarative and testable outside the mapper, while the mapper translates the Specification into the appropriate query language (SQL, JPQL, LINQ).
related_patterns_notes.assembler: Companion distribution pattern: Assembler (also called DTO Mapper) builds Data Transfer Objects from domain objects, typically for API or service-layer responses. While a Data Mapper translates between domain and relational rows, an Assembler translates between domain and flat/external DTOs. In layered systems the Data Mapper often delegates to an Assembler for the read path (domain → DTO for the wire) while the Data Mapper handles the write path (DTO → domain for commands). Keep Assembler in the application/infrastructure layer, not the domain.
related_patterns_notes.cqrs: Sister pattern: CQRS separates read and write models into different object structures. Data Mapper translates both paths — the write path (domain → rows) and the read path (rows → read-model DTOs/projections). In CQRS, the Data Mapper's per-aggregate interface remains, but read queries bypass it and use projections or query objects directly, preventing change-tracker overhead on the read path.
related_patterns_notes.event-sourcing: Companion pattern: in event-sourced systems the aggregate is reconstituted by replaying events rather than by loading a snapshot. The Data Mapper serves as a projection target: it translates event-sourced state (serialised or reconstructed domain objects) into relational rows for storage, and the same mapper interface can hydrate domain objects from rows for backwards-compatible legacy reads.
related_patterns_notes.outbox-pattern: Supporting pattern for reliable event publication: the Data Mapper flushes business entities plus an outbox event record in the same transaction, and a separate process reads the outbox and publishes events. This decouples the mapper's transactional write from external delivery guarantees without two-phase commit.
